g.text: LIST fights the shard key - so it gets its own table, ordered differently
hash(bucket_id, object_key) is perfect for GET and destroys lexicographic locality by design, which is exactly what LIST needs.
Bucket names are unique across ALL tenants, so creation must
serialize globally. The one truly global constraint here - and
the reason this table cannot be sharded.
version_id is a TIMEUUID - unique AND sortable at once.
It is LAST in the key, so all versions of one object
share a partition: flipping is_latest is a single-shard,
two-row transaction with no distributed commit.
bucket_id and object_key are REDUNDANT here - they
exist purely so this co-shards with objects, making
'row + ordered part list' a single-shard two-table
read rather than a cross-shard join.
An object's data is legitimately NON-CONTIGUOUS:
multipart assembly is a metadata stitch, not a copy.
Against objects, sharded on hash(bucket, key):
Hashing DESTROYS lexicographic locality, so keys sharing a prefix scatter
across every shard. Fan out to all, merge-sort in the API service, return 1,000.
And pagination cannot be an offset - 'next 1,000 after X' re-queries every
shard again. With 64 shards that is 64 queries PER PAGE.
The fix: a denormalized read model
Sharded on bucket_id ALONE, clustered on
live on ONE shard, in lexicographic order.
A prefix list becomes a single-shard range scan,
and pagination is just continuing that scan.
CQRS applied to a schema: a write-optimized
table plus a read-optimized projection, fed by CDC.
LIST becomes EVENTUALLY CONSISTENT - a just-uploaded object may not appear for a
second, while GET on it works immediately. Real object stores behave exactly this way.
A hot shard per hot bucket, since one bucket's rows are all co-located.
And it makes listing a billion keys POSSIBLE, not fast - a million sequential pages is
a million requests however well indexed. Listing is slow by construction.
Only the pointer needs strong consistency
objects (one row) strong, read-after-write - but the shard key is derivable from (bucket, key), so no distributed transaction
is_latest invariant strong, single-shard, two rows in one partition - guaranteed by key column order, not by a commit protocol
object BYTES written and confirmed durable BEFORE metadata commits, then immutable - so no consistency question arises
S3 was eventually consistent for overwrites until 2020, and this schema shows why: strong read-after-write needs a key's reads routed
to a replica holding its latest commit. That expensive guarantee is bought on a 0.7 TB store rather than a 100 PB one - three orders
of magnitude cheaper, and the payoff of splitting name from bytes showing up somewhere non-obvious.
